## 💡 What is Univer?

**Univer** is an Office SDK for building Office applications inside your own product. It provides Office editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing for people and existing agents, using your data and permissions. The product family covers spreadsheets, documents, presentations, relational tables, canvases, and PDFs.

Univer Office SDK has three parts: - **Web SDK** is the foundation: content models, editing, rendering, formula calculation, and Facade APIs (application-facing APIs). Compose its plugins into an embedded editor or your own Office application, and reuse the content models, commands, and calculation for Headless processing without an interactive editor. - **Server SDK** adds backend services for real-time collaboration, edit history, and Office file import and export. - **AI SDK** connects Office capabilities to existing agents and workflows, with content tools, execution, and review integrations. **This repository provides the Web SDK's core architecture and engine implementations under Apache-2.0**: content models and snapshot formats, plugin and dependency management, the command system, formula and rendering engines, Facade APIs, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs editing capabilities. Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and commercial AI SDK extensions are distributed and licensed separately. Agents can use the same open-source APIs; your application supplies the model and tool orchestration. The [quotation example](#connect-your-application-to-editable-content) demonstrates editing, calculation, and saving without an AI SDK dependency. ### Open-source capabilities
Area Selected capabilities
Sheets · Editing and layout Cell styles, merged cells, in-cell rich text, freeze panes, floating images, and undo/redo.
Sheets · Data and calculation Formulas, defined names, filtering, sorting, data validation, conditional formatting, hyperlinks, comments, and find and replace.
Docs Rich-text editing, paragraph formatting, lists, hyperlinks, comments, and drawing integration.
Features are composed through plugins and presets; the [quick start](#quick-start) uses only the **Sheets Core preset**. Images use the corresponding drawing plugins. See the [feature comparison](https://univer.ai/compare/) for detailed open-source and commercial coverage. The demos below showcase the wider **Univer Office SDK**, including commercial capabilities. They show more than the default open-source setup; see [open source and commercial extensions](#open-source-and-commercial-extensions) for scope.

## 🚀 Build on the open-source foundation

Your goal Use the open-source foundation Start here
Embed Sheets or Docs Add an editable Office surface to your application or agent product, and connect your data through Facade APIs. Quick start
Process content without an editor Reuse content plugins, models, commands, and calculation in Node.js for editing, snapshots, and automated tasks. Headless guide
Develop custom features or editors Reuse the engines, UI components, plugin boundaries, dependency injection, and command/undo systems. Follow existing features to extend Sheets and Docs or develop your own editors. Open-source architecture
**Coordinate edits and undo/redo across features.** Inserting a row inside a filter range changes both the base content and the filter range; undo needs to restore both. Each feature supplies its own changes and undo data, and the command composes their execution and history. The architecture walkthrough explains how to extend these editing workflows. ### Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor In a browser application using a bundler such as Vite: ```bash pnpm add @univerjs/presets @univerjs/preset-sheets-core ``` Create the container before initializing Univer: ```html
``` ```ts import { UniverSheetsCorePreset } from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core' import UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/locales/en-US' import { createUniver, LocaleType, mergeLocales } from '@univerjs/presets' import '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/lib/index.css' const { univerAPI } = createUniver({ locale: LocaleType.EN_US, locales: { [LocaleType.EN_US]: mergeLocales(UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS), }, presets: [ UniverSheetsCorePreset({ container: 'app', }), ], }) univerAPI.createWorkbook({}) ``` Your page now contains a spreadsheet editor. Use the returned `univerAPI` to work with its content. This example uses open-source packages and needs no commercial Univer license or Server SDK. For component frameworks, retain the `univer` instance returned by `createUniver` and call `univer.dispose()` when the component unmounts. See the [lifecycle guide](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/lifecycle). Presets compose plugins and register their Facade APIs. For manual control, see the [Plugin Mode example](#manual-plugin-composition) below. The [installation guide](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/installation) covers both modes, peer dependencies, and framework integrations. Keep coordinated `@univerjs/*` packages on the same version. Commercial packages must use the matching release line; independently released packages such as icons follow their declared compatibility. See the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md). ### Connect your application to editable content Facade APIs are the application-facing interface to workbooks, worksheets, and ranges. Continue from the quick start to populate a quotation, update a quantity from application code, and read the recalculated total: ```ts // Wait for formula controllers before editing a newly created workbook. await new Promise((resolve) => { if (univerAPI.getCurrentLifecycleStage() >= univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) { resolve() return } const listener = univerAPI.addEvent(univerAPI.Event.LifeCycleChanged, ({ stage }) => { if (stage === univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) { listener.dispose() resolve() } }) }) const workbook = univerAPI.getActiveWorkbook()! const sheet = workbook.getActiveSheet() sheet.getRange('A1:D4').setValues([ ['Item', 'Quantity', 'Unit price', 'Amount'], ['Seats', 2, 25, '=B2*C2'], ['Support', 1, 100, '=B3*C3'], ['Total', '', '', '=SUM(D2:D3)'], ]) // An application control or agent can make the same edit. sheet.getRange('B2').setValue(4) univerAPI.getFormula().onCalculationResultApplied().then(() => { console.log(sheet.getRange('D4').getValue()) // 200 localStorage.setItem('quotation', JSON.stringify(workbook.save())) }).catch(console.error) ``` The editor and your application operate on the same workbook; formula changes are recalculated automatically. `workbook.save()` returns a JSON snapshot containing the workbook and its registered plugin data. Your application owns persistence; this example uses browser storage. On a later page load, after initialization, restore the snapshot **instead of creating a blank workbook**: ```ts const saved = localStorage.getItem('quotation') if (saved) { univerAPI.createWorkbook(JSON.parse(saved)) } ``` This workflow uses only open-source packages. Snapshot persistence is separate from XLSX import and export, which uses the separately distributed file-conversion capabilities. Use public Facade APIs for application integration; the source links below explain internal implementation and extension points. See the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md) before depending on an extension point.
Advanced: compose plugins manually (Plugin Mode) Use Plugin Mode when you need precise control over plugin selection, dependencies, or loading. The preset above handles this composition for you. This alternative initialization uses the same `app` container and the Sheets Core preset's browser plugin stack without a Worker. ## 🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture

### Give custom features clear boundaries Univer organizes content logic and UI interaction in separate plugins. Feature plugins manage rules and content changes; UI plugins provide the interface and user interactions. For example, `sheets-filter` manages filter ranges and rules, while `sheets-filter-ui` provides panels, menus, and shortcuts. ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% A layered overview, not a complete dependency graph. %% Group arrows indicate reuse of the layer below; internal arrows show selected dependencies. flowchart TD subgraph FEATURES["Feature Plugins"] direction LR FUI["Filter
UI Plugin"] VUI["Data Validation
UI Plugin"] FILTER["Filter Plugin"] VALIDATION["Data Validation Plugin"] FUI --> FILTER VUI --> VALIDATION end subgraph PRODUCTS["Product Plugins"] direction LR SUI["Sheets UI Plugin"] SHEETS["Sheets Plugin"] SUI --> SHEETS end subgraph FOUNDATION["Core Framework & Plugins"] direction LR UI["UI Plugin"] FORMULA["Formula Engine Plugin"] RENDER["Render Engine Plugin"] CORE["Core"] UI --> RENDER RENDER --> CORE FORMULA --> CORE end FEATURES --> PRODUCTS PRODUCTS --> FOUNDATION classDef logic fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef ui fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px classDef shared fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef feature fill:#172d50,color:#ffffff,stroke:#172d50 class FUI,VUI ui class FILTER,VALIDATION logic class SUI,SHEETS logic class UI,FORMULA,RENDER,CORE shared style FEATURES fill:#f7fcf9,stroke:#b5d8c1,color:#17543a style PRODUCTS fill:#f5f9ff,stroke:#b6cbea,color:#17365f style FOUNDATION fill:#fafbfc,stroke:#cbd2dc,color:#334155 ``` **Figure 1: three plugin layers.** Feature plugins build on product plugins, which reuse the core framework and plugins. Group arrows show dependencies on the layer below; Core provides content models, commands, dependency injection, and lifecycle management. Some plugins and dependencies are omitted. New features keep their rules in their own plugins and cooperate through public services, commands, and defined extension points. UI plugins build on shared UI services and components. Dependencies are explicit at two levels: - **Between plugins:** `DependentOn` declares runtime plugin dependencies. The plugin service orders them, and lifecycle stages separate dependency registration, content initialization, and UI initialization. - **Inside plugins:** dependency injection connects controllers and services through declared dependencies. Supported overrides let an application replace an implementation, adapt a platform service, or supply a test double. Instance-scoped injectors keep application state separate between Univer instances. Disposable registration also gives commands, listeners, components, and icons a cleanup path when their owner is disposed. The [filter plugin](./packages/sheets-filter/src/plugin.ts) and its [UI plugin](./packages/sheets-filter-ui/src/plugin.ts) show these boundaries in working code.
Inside a feature: Model, Controller, Service, and the UI foundation For filtering, `sheets-filter` owns content logic and `sheets-filter-ui` owns UI interaction. Each module has a focused responsibility. ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% Every arrow means contains. Arrows mean “contains.”** Both plugins can contain Controllers and Services: logic Controllers coordinate content changes and related features; UI Controllers connect menus, shortcuts, and interactions, with UI Services managing panel state. These responsibilities give new features a consistent structure to implement and test. The UI foundation follows the same division. **`@univerjs/design`** supplies shared components and styles, **`@univerjs/ui`** provides workbench services such as menus, shortcuts, panels, and component registration, and **`@univerjs/icons`** supplies icons. A feature registers its components and icons, contributes menus, and attaches its rendering through these extension points. Teams can add a panel or toolbar feature while reusing the application's UI infrastructure. See the [UI overview](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/ui/overview) and the filter plugin's [component and icon registration](./packages/sheets-filter-ui/src/controllers/components.controller.ts).
### Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo For example, when rows are inserted inside a filter range, the filter plugin supplies the corresponding range change and its undo data. The row command composes the base edit and participating feature changes, executes them, and records their undo/redo information together. The row insertion feature can use the shared extension mechanism while the filter plugin owns its range-update rules. The command system distinguishes three kinds of action: - **Command** orchestrates a business action and the changes it requires. - **Mutation** changes content saved in a snapshot, with serializable parameters. - **Operation** changes transient state, such as an open panel or the scroll position. **A shared structure for undo/redo.** For an undoable edit, the feature implementation supplies the forward mutations and corresponding inverse mutations, and the Command records them through `IUndoRedoService`. When one action affects several features, the Command can combine their changes and undo data in a single undo/redo record, so the user can undo and redo the complete action. See [extending commands](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/custom-command). Features still need to cooperate. **Interceptors and reference-range handlers give that cooperation a defined place.** At supported extension points, plugins contribute checks or related mutations; interceptor priorities control ordering where the API defines it.
Example: commands, callbacks, feature coordination, and undo/redo ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% Simplified insert-row example. A command composes mutations and records undo after success. %% Events may also fire for nested command executions; not every callback is drawn. flowchart TD BEFORE["Before execution
Inspect or cancel"] CMD["Insert-row Command"] BASE["Row mutations"] EXT["Feature extension points
Filter range changes"] MODEL["Execute combined mutations"] UNDO["Record undo and redo"] AFTER["After execution
Notify listeners"] BEFORE --> CMD CMD --> BASE CMD --> EXT BASE --> MODEL EXT --> MODEL MODEL --> UNDO UNDO --> AFTER classDef entry fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef core fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef extension fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px class BEFORE,AFTER entry class CMD,BASE,MODEL,UNDO core class EXT extension ``` This diagram simplifies an insert-row workflow. Nested command executions have their own callbacks; it does not show every event or the separate Operation path. See the [row command](./packages/sheets/src/commands/commands/insert-row-col.command.ts), [filter controller](./packages/sheets-filter/src/controllers/sheets-filter.controller.ts), and [interceptor service](./packages/sheets/src/services/sheet-interceptor/sheet-interceptor.service.ts).
These boundaries support a practical testing strategy: test models and services independently, replace external dependencies through DI, and add regression cases for combined actions and undo/redo. The [filter controller tests](./packages/sheets-filter/src/controllers/__tests__/sheets-filter.controller.spec.ts) exercise row and column changes and their effect on filtering. ### Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events The repository includes the content models, formula engine, and Canvas rendering and layout engine behind the editors. They are shared building blocks: spreadsheet rich text, for example, reuses document layout and rendering. Custom features can build on these engines instead of implementing a separate content stack. Read about the [formula engine architecture](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/formula) and [rendering engine architecture](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/rendering). Browser editors, Node.js Headless tasks, and appropriately composed Workers can reuse the corresponding content plugins, models, commands, and calculation. See [Headless Univer](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/node) and the [isomorphic architecture](./docs/ISOMORPHIC.md). `ICommandService` exposes execution callbacks so plugins can observe commands before and after execution. Facade APIs wrap the underlying capabilities in application objects such as `FWorkbook`, `FWorksheet`, and `FRange`. Each plugin contributes its own Facade extensions, **typed events through `univerAPI.Event`**, and **enums through `univerAPI.Enum`**. Application code can discover event names and constants from one entry point instead of importing private services or repeating strings. For example, `BeforeCommandExecute` can inspect and cancel an execution; `CommandExecuted` reports executions to listeners. Listeners return disposables, and cancellation applies where the event supports it. Facade extensions stay with their feature packages, so a content API does not have to pull in unrelated UI APIs. See the [Facade design](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/facade), [command callbacks and event bridge](./packages/core/src/facade/f-univer.ts), and [Enum entry point](./packages/core/src/facade/f-enum.ts). The repository provides working feature implementations and patterns for extending them. Read the [filter implementation walkthrough](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/anatomy) for a complete example, or the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md) before depending on an extension point.

## 🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK

When you want more ready-to-integrate capabilities, compose the corresponding **Univer Office SDK** modules: additional content types, advanced editing plugins, collaboration, file conversion, and agent tooling. They extend the same content models, plugin architecture, command system, and Facade design introduced above, so you can build on your existing integration.
Part How it extends the foundation
Open-source Web SDK core · this repository Open-source models, engines, plugins, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs capabilities, with corresponding Headless content operations. Use them in commercial applications under Apache-2.0.
Commercial Web SDK plugins Follow the core's Plugin, dependency injection, Command/Mutation, and Facade extension patterns. Add charts, shapes, pivot tables, SmartArt, and other features for the corresponding content types.
Server SDK Extends the same content models and mutation conventions with real-time collaboration, revision history, and Office file conversion. Integrates with your application's identity, permissions, and storage.
AI SDK extensions Reuse Web SDK Headless and Facade capabilities to provide composable Node.js APIs and CLI building blocks for agents to inspect, edit, and check content, with collaboration and Worktree review integrations.
### Scope and licensing - **This repository:** Apache-2.0 packages that can be used in commercial applications under that license, including the open-source Headless content capabilities. - **Commercial extensions:** Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and AI SDK capabilities beyond the open-source foundation are distributed and licensed separately. **Freemium** evaluation includes watermarks and feature limits. - **Reference applications:** Open-source applications such as Univer Workspace have their own source licenses. Their SDK dependencies retain their respective licenses. See the [feature comparison](https://univer.ai/compare/), including its **Open source only** filter, for detailed coverage and [plans and licensing](https://univer.ai/pricing/) for commercial options.
How shared content models connect editing, collaboration, and files These capabilities operate on serializable **Unit snapshots**, including Sheets' `IWorkbookData`, Docs' `IDocumentData`, Slides' `ISlideData`, and canvases' `IBoardData` (called **Boards** in the API). These types come from core and the respective product packages; current Slides and Boards capabilities are separately distributed commercial products. The shared Unit conventions let browser editors, backend services, and agents work with the same content. Commands orchestrate edits; **Mutations describe content changes**. Collaboration packages those mutations into **changesets**, applies **operational transformation (OT)** to concurrent changes, and manages confirmed revisions and snapshots. History can reconstruct a revision from a snapshot and subsequent changesets. Read the [collaboration design](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/ot) and [Collaboration SDK overview](https://docs.univer.ai/server/collaboration/overview). **Exchange** maps Office file structures to and from Univer content snapshots. For OOXML formats such as **XLSX, DOCX, and PPTX**, it parses the file into the corresponding Sheet, Doc, or Slide data and generates the file representation on export. The converted content can enter the same editing, calculation, collaboration, and agent workflows. See [Office file import and export](https://docs.univer.ai/server/import-export/node).
How AI SDK gives agents the same content capabilities AI SDK builds on the Web SDK's **Headless content models, commands, calculation, and Facade APIs**. It exposes structured TypeScript APIs and optional Commander presets that applications can compose into their own Office CLI or agent tools. - **Understand, discover, and edit.** Inspection returns structured content. API Reference helps the agent find Facade symbols and signatures shipped with its SDK. Facade execution distinguishes read and write modes, captures mutations, and works with explicit synchronization and commit results. See [content operations](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/content-operations). - **Check the rendered result.** A browser Render Runtime reuses Web SDK rendering for screenshots. Slide layout lint adds structured findings for issues such as off-page or overlapping text, giving the agent evidence for another editing pass. See [visual inspection](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/visual-inspection). - **Edit drafts for human review.** With the corresponding collaboration and Web capabilities, agents can edit and verify an isolated Worktree draft over several rounds, then hand it to a person to review, merge, or reopen. The workflow uses the same snapshots, mutations, and revision conventions. See [Worktree](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/worktree). For repeated calls, optional [Worker pools and a daemon](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/runtime-architecture) reuse loaded content instances and reduce repeated initialization. Your application owns the root CLI, targets, authorization, and output. Explore the [AI SDK package catalog](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/packages) to select the required capabilities.

## 🌐 Application patterns and ecosystem

### Univer Workspace: an Office SDK reference application For a complete application reference, start with [Univer Workspace](https://github.com/dream-num/univer-workspace). It shows how to compose Univer Office SDK editors, collaboration, file capabilities, existing agents, and human review into a self-hostable workspace. Follow its integration patterns when building your own Office application or agent workspace.

Univer is compiled with a Chrome 88 target and aims to work with the versions listed above.

### Runtime compatibility - **Polyfills**: Univer relies on `Intl.Segmenter`. Add a polyfill such as `@formatjs/intl-segmenter` if your target browser or runtime does not provide it. - **Build tools**: We recommend Vite, esbuild, or Webpack 5. If your build tool does not support the `exports` field in `package.json` (common in Webpack 4), you may need extra path mapping. - **React**: Univer's view layer is built on React 18, supports React 18 and 19, and provides minimal compatibility support for React 16.9+ and 17. - **Node.js runtime**: Headless Univer supports Node.js `>=18.17.0`. Developing this monorepo requires Node.js `>=22.18`.
Developing in this repository ### Repository layout ```text . ├── packages/ Core packages, engines, document types, UI plugins, and feature plugins ├── examples/ All-in-one Vite workbench used for local browser development ├── common/ Shared internal tooling, storybook, and utilities ├── tests/ Additional integration test projects └── docs/ Architecture notes, images, and repository-local documentation ``` Package-level READMEs live beside each package under [`packages/`](./packages). ### Local development Requirements: - Node.js `>=22.18` - pnpm: use the version declared by `packageManager` in `package.json`. ```bash git clone https://github.com/dream-num/univer.git cd univer pnpm install pnpm dev ``` Useful commands:

repositories.readme:
# Modern Web Guidance (Source) This repo is the source repository for [GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance) and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents. [**Modern Web Guidance**](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) and [GOVERNANCE.md](./GOVERNANCE.md) for how we work on the project and orientation of the codebase. --- *Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.* [Documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) · [Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/) · [Source Code](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src) · [Report an Issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues) ## Quickstart ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install ``` This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See [Alternative Installation Methods](#-alternative-installation-methods) below. #### Try it out (without installing) ```shell # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer" # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . ``` ## Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. **Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: * **Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. * **Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. ## What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. ### Core Disciplines

🎨 User Experience

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).

📐 CSS Layout

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

⚡ Performance

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).

📝 Forms & UI

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

♿ Accessibility

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

🤖 Built-in AI

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
_View an example:_ [the `navigation-drawer` guide](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-components/navigation-drawer.md). #### The full list

### Safe Adoption of Modern Features * **Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks**: We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles. * **Gotchas & Quirks**: We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for `fetchLater()` or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors. * **Baseline-Aware Integration**: We leverage real-time compatibility data from the **Baseline** project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support. * **Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates**: Guides covering experimental **Origin Trial** APIs or **volatile features** (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via `search`, but are gated on `retrieve` so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent. ### Project Configuration (`.mwgrc`) Configure Origin Trial and volatile feature opt-ins for a repository with an optional `.mwgrc` JSON file in your project root (or `~/.mwgrc` as a user-level fallback), which you can commit to share across your team: | CLI Command | `.mwgrc` Key | Effect | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-origin-trials` | `"allowOriginTrials": true` | Unlocks guides for experimental Origin Trial APIs. | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-volatile-features` | `"allowVolatileFeatures": true` | Unlocks guides for volatile single-engine features. | ## How It Works 1. **Activation**: The coding agent activates the `modern-web-guidance` skill because of a relevant task. The agent is instructed to use the `modern-web-guidance` CLI for web platform queries. 2. **Local Semantic Search**: The agent runs `modern-web-guidance search ""`. The tool matches the query to the best guide using an offline, zero-dependency embedding model and BM25 search engine (no network calls, no API keys). 3. **Guide Fetch**: The agent retrieves the guide via `modern-web-guidance retrieve `, inserting targeted code patterns, gotchas, and fallbacks directly into its context window. > [!TIP] > Note: We use `npx` to ensure the content doesn't go stale, but the CLI works offline, completely private and local. > The npm package is self-contained, with no extra dependencies to ensure both low-latency and supply-chain security. ## Alternative Installation Methods

Otherwise, consult your agent's documentation for updating plugins and skills. ## Evals to prove this works well We developed a robust eval harness to ensure that the content is **empirically proven and continuously calibrated** so AI agents write better code. We run automated evaluations using a closed-loop validation pipeline: ``` [ Expert-authored guidance and demo ] │ ▼ [ Target generation ] ──> Tasks on real webapps, Golden solutions, Playwright graders │ ▼ [ Calibration loop ] ───> Runs Grader on Golden Solutions (Must Pass 100%) │ Runs Grader on Unmodified Base App (Must Fail 100%) ▼ [ E2E agent evals ] ────> Runs coding agents in guided vs. unguided modes Compares pass rates and accessibility w/ and w/o the skill ``` 1. **Simulated Developer Tasks**: We define realistic developer prompts against full base applications (`daily-grind`, `devtools-times`) that mimic real-world requests (e.g., "make my images load faster"). Prompts avoid naming APIs or features, testing whether the agent can naturally discover and apply the right guides. 2. **Static & Browser-Based Checks**: Playwright graders verify that each implementation requirement was followed—checking source patterns, computed styles, runtime DOM behaviors, and accessibility states. 3. **Self-Healing Calibration**: Graders are calibrated against multi-agent (Claude/Codex/AGY) golden solutions (100% pass target) and an unmodified baseline application (0% pass target). 4. **E2E Testing**: We measure coding agent performance on real tasks with and without guidance. The _opportunity_ (100% - unguided pass rate) and _uplift_ (guided - unguided pass rate) are key: if models already succeed without guidance, we prune redundant advice; where agents struggle, we refine guides to maximize uplift. ### Recent eval results snapshot Explore full per-agent and per-guide breakdowns on the **[Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/)**. | Date | Agent + Model | Tasks / Checks | Unguided → Guided (Uplift) | | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | | Nov 8 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 214 / 1673 | 58% → 94% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 8 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 215 / 1795 | 54% → 82% (**+28pp**) | | Nov 8 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 215 / 1801 | 57% → 88% (**+31pp**) | | Nov 6 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 212 / 1773 | 53% → 86% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 6 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 212 / 1773 | 56% → 90% (**+34pp**) | | Nov 6 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 212 / 1722 | 60% → 96% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 4 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 209 / 1743 | 52% → 85% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 4 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 209 / 1743 | 57% → 90% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 4 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 207 / 1722 | 60% → 96% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 2 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 205 / 1729 | 55% → 82% (**+27pp**) | ## Available Skill Packs You can customize which skill packs are installed using the `--choose` flag: ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install --choose ``` * **`modern-web-guidance`** (~205 tokens): Comprehensive guidance on modern browser APIs, layouts, and performance. * **`chrome-extensions`** (~175 tokens): Guidance on Manifest V3, background workers, extension APIs, and Chrome Web Store publishing. ## Telemetry & Privacy Google collects anonymous usage information to improve the tool's reliability, relevance, and performance. repositories.name: LoopForge
repositories.description: Self-hosted workflows for coding-agent delivery. Orchestrate CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code with scripts and human approval gates. Includes Local workflows for coding assistants.
repositories.readme:
English · 简体中文

Two ways to work · Quick start · SOPs · Features · Local · FAQ · Docs

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8af401d9-1aae-427c-b4bc-455c12d17beb

80-second product tour (1080p, with sound).

**LoopForge** is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to **Main Bot** in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as an **SOP** (a standard workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in. Coding-agent CLIs do the work: CodeBuddy, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Pi, DeepSeek Harness and ZCode. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license. ## Two ways to work | | **Chat with Main Bot** | **Run an SOP** | | --- | --- | --- | | Best for | Exploring, quick fixes, iterating with the agent | Repeatable delivery with fixed stages and sign-off | | How it runs | Main Bot opens a [conversation workspace](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) (a Docker sandbox with your repos) on demand and calls project roles as subagents | The engine runs Agent, Script, Human-gate and sub-SOP nodes in order, in their own sandbox | | You stay in control by | Queuing or steering messages mid-reply, and pausing, resuming or taking over a running SOP from chat | Approving at human gates, sending work back to a chosen step, retrying or rerunning from any node | | Delivers | A PR/MR, or a direct merge into a shared branch (`mode=direct`) | Documents, code or a PR, plus per-node artifacts and logs | Both paths track the same **requirements**, so every change, whether made in chat or by an SOP, links back to what was asked for and counts toward delivery and cost reports.

The chat home. Type a request, @ a role, skill, requirement, SOP or repository, and pick the executor, model and permission mode per conversation.

## Why LoopForge Ask a coding agent to "fix this bug" and the result depends on that run. It might skip the plan, forget the tests, review its own code, or stop halfway without anyone noticing. That's fine for a demo, but it isn't how a team ships. - **Repeatable.** Same SOP, same stages, same checks for every requirement. Start from built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs. - **Separated roles.** Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools. A role works as an SOP node or as a subagent in chat. - **Human in the loop.** Approval gates where they matter. Read the report, approve, or send the work back to a chosen step. - **Observable and resumable.** Node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts in one place. Pause, retry a failed step, or rerun from any node. - **Your stack, your servers.** Ten coding-agent CLIs as executors, from CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code to OpenCode, Cursor CLI and more. GitHub, Skills and MCP as tools. Docker sandboxes or your own machine as the runtime. ## Quick start Install **Git** and clone the repository first. The installer checks Docker, Compose, Python 3 and curl and offers to install missing components. Python/curl installation supports apt, dnf and yum on Linux; the Compose plugin supports x86_64/arm64 and verifies the official release SHA-256. macOS needs a working Python 3 and Docker Desktop; Homebrew can install missing components. Ordinary Linux users are supported through Docker group access or sudo. Set `LOOPFORGE_YES=1` to accept installation prompts. Package and image downloads require internet access. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git cd LoopForge ./start.sh ``` `./start.sh` pulls the GHCR release image pinned in `compose.yaml` without building locally (`bash scripts/install.sh` does the same). It creates the MySQL and platform services, generates configuration and session secrets, and installs the built-in sandboxes, starter SOPs and welcome project. Host Go and Node.js installations are not required. Configure model API keys and GitHub authorization after startup. Use `./start.sh logs`, `stop`, `restart` or `pull` to manage it, and `./start.sh dev` to build the checkout from source. If downloads from `ghcr.io` stall, set `MIRROR` to a registry host that can stand in for `ghcr.io`. `./start.sh` pulls from that host and tags the image back to the name pinned in `compose.yaml`. Setting `MIRROR` trusts that host, because the download is tagged with the official name. The GitHub Release records the digest; `docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge:` should show the same digest after `@`. Without `MIRROR`, `./start.sh` still pulls `ghcr.io` directly, and `compose.yaml` stays unchanged. Upgrade with the same variable and `./start.sh pull`. [ghcr.nju.edu.cn](https://doc.nju.edu.cn/books/e1654/page/ghcr) is one such host. A Docker `registry-mirrors` entry such as `https://docker.nju.edu.cn` only accelerates Docker Hub and is not a value for `MIRROR`. ```bash MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn ./start.sh ``` Open the address printed by the installer and create your account; the first one becomes the administrator. The service listens on `0.0.0.0:8090` by default. On a cloud host, the installer reads the public IP from the provider's metadata service and prints it; allow the port in your security group, or put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front. Restrict access to your own IP until the administrator account exists. The home page's quick-access guide walks you through adding a model key, connecting a repository and choosing an SOP. For GitLab, Gitea, Gogs and other Git hosts, [set up Git SSH](docs/deployment.md#git-repositories-over-ssh) to check out and push branches with a personal key. PR/MR and Issue automation requires a hosting API token or a separately configured MCP. ### Try it without an API key New accounts join the **LoopForge demo project**, which includes an SOP made only of a script and a human gate: 1. Switch to the demo project, open **Templates**, and open **Platform check · script & approval**. 2. Click **Run SOP**. A real script writes a report, then the run waits for you at the approval step. 3. Approve it from **Needs review** or the run page, and watch the run continue to its final artifact. ### What you need for real work | I want to… | You need | | --- | --- | | Run the script + approval demo | Nothing | | Chat with Main Bot, generate a document or a new project | An API key for the selected executor | | Change an existing repository (in chat or via an SOP) and open a PR | Model credentials and a GitHub repository (connect GitHub in personal settings) |
More setup details: executors, GitHub, sandboxes, access model
- **Executors.** Pick one of ten CLIs beside the home composer, then a model. Every SOP role can choose its executor independently (built-in roles default to CodeBuddy). Requirement clarification, AI notification summaries, Bot replies and run evals currently use CodeBuddy, so their model pickers list CodeBuddy models only and the server refuses a model of another CLI instead of switching it to CodeBuddy; scheduled assistant tasks run on the CLI the task selects. | Executor | Credentials | Installation | | --- | --- | --- | | **CodeBuddy** | Personal key, or a shared key an administrator configures for chat and SOP runs | In the Docker image | | **Codex** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | In the Docker image | | **Claude Code** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **OpenCode · Kimi Code · Pi** | Personal key only | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **DeepSeek Harness** | Personal key only | In the Docker image | | **Cursor CLI · Antigravity** | Personal key only | Provider installer on first chat use; not installed into SOP sandboxes | | **ZCode** | Personal key only | Not bundled; install it on the service or execution machine PATH | The seven agent CLIs after Claude Code keep their model and MCP configuration in a private home directory per run, so they always use the responsible user's own key and Base URL from personal settings, even on a connected execution machine. When rolling them out to a team, each member configures their own credentials. First-use installs need npm or provider access; [native deployments](docs/deployment.md#workers-and-runners) need the CLI for the executor you choose. - **GitHub is optional.** All built-in generic SOPs run without a repository: product SOPs deliver documents, and new frontend/backend projects deliver source files in the task workspace. Bug fixes still need source code and reproduction details. Connect a repository when you work on existing code or want PRs. - **Delivering to a repository.** Choose **Connect GitHub** in personal settings, approve the device code on GitHub and pick your repository (the LoopForge OAuth App is built in; no PAT required, manual PAT entry still works). Set executor credentials (or bind a local execution machine), then either run a project SOP or ask Main Bot to change the code and submit a PR/MR. - **Sandboxes.** In the default Compose installation, SOP runs and conversation workspaces both use Docker sandbox containers started through the host Docker socket. Default sandboxes reuse the installed runtime image, so nothing extra is built after installation; custom Dockerfiles still build their own images. Docker socket access grants control of the host daemon, so this setup is for trusted teams, not untrusted multi-tenant isolation. See [deployment boundaries](docs/deployment.md#accounts). Re-running the installer keeps your data. - **Accounts and access.** New installations listen on all interfaces (existing bind settings are kept) and are designed for a trusted team: signed-in users can read project data across the instance, and teammates can sign up from the login page (`AGENTFLOW_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false` in `.env` turns that off). Read the [account and access model](docs/deployment.md#accounts) before exposing it beyond your team. - **Remote access, HTTPS, separate workers.** See [Deployment](docs/deployment.md). - **Hacking on LoopForge itself?** `bash scripts/dev.sh` runs it natively (Go 1.26.11+).
## How SOPs work An **SOP** is the workflow a delivery follows. Agents, scripts and people take part in the same run:

The SOP designer with the built-in bug-fix SOP. Each step picks a role; failed checks can send the work back to an earlier step.

| Node | What it does | | --- | --- | | **Agent** | A role (prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools) that designs, implements, reviews or tests. | | **Script** | A deterministic shell step: build, test, lint, generate a report. No AI where AI is not needed. | | **Human gate** | Pauses the run until someone checks the artifacts and approves, or sends the work back to a step. | | **Sub-SOP** | Runs another SOP as a sub-workflow. | | **Preview build** | Builds a static site and archives it for review. | Each node declares its artifacts and dependencies, and the engine starts each step once its dependencies complete. Start from a built-in SOP, adapt its roles, rules and environment to your project, and publish versions as it evolves.

A run waiting at a human gate: approve and continue, add context and rerun the step, or send the work back upstream.

**A delivery we actually ran:** four CodeBuddy roles planned a Python fix, implemented it, reviewed it independently and summarized the delivery. Three real tests passed; the run waited for human approval, then verified the accepted code had not changed. The [reusable acceptance case](e2e/api/45-delivery-model.test.mjs) checks the files and results. See the [validation record](docs/validation.md) for scope and known gaps. ## Features | Area | What you get | | --- | --- | | **Chat workbench** | Main Bot with per-conversation executor, model and permission mode. `@` references for roles, skills, requirements, SOPs and repositories. Messages queue while a reply runs; *Steer* interrupts and sends now. Generated files open in a side panel with preview, source and download. | | **Conversation workspaces** | On-demand Docker sandboxes with the project's repositories checked out, project roles as native subagents, and direct control of a running SOP workspace: pause, resume or take over. | | **SOP designer** | Visual canvas with Agent, Script, Human gate, Sub-SOP and Preview nodes, rework-on-failure edges, validation, version history and publishing. Built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs. | | **Roles** | Reusable definitions: prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills, MCP tools, artifacts and gates, shared across SOP nodes and chat subagents. | | **Requirement → delivery** | Requirements tracked end to end, whether shipped by an SOP or straight from chat, with PR/MR status tracking, merge detection and direct-branch merges. | | **Runs & approvals** | Live node status, tool traces, worker logs, per-node artifact snapshots and workspace previews. A single **Needs review** inbox for every gate waiting on you. | | **AI scheduled tasks** | Recurring agent tasks with full workspace, SOP and MCP access; a shared market of versioned, parameterized task templates; automatic SOP dispatch for new requirements. | | **Insights & cost** | Engineering metrics, business-domain reports with static HTML/SVG export, and token/cost accounting for SOPs and conversations at public list prices. | | **Execution environments** | Platform workers, Docker sandboxes, or a connected local execution machine using your own tools and repositories. | | **Team-ready** | Password accounts, projects and members, light/dark/system themes, an OpenAPI-described HTTP and MCP API. Management pages are in English and Chinese; the chat workbench is Chinese for now. |

Built-in SOPs are read-only blueprints; copy one into your project to run and edit it.

## LoopForge Local Don't want to run a server? **LoopForge Local** brings the built-in delivery workflows straight into the coding assistant you already use: ```bash # Run inside your target project, e.g. for Claude Code npx -y loopforge-cli@latest install claude ``` Then run `/start-devflow ""` in Claude Code. | Host | Supported | | --- | --- | | Claude Code · CodeBuddy · Codex · Cursor | Classic (default) and Portable editions | | Pi | Portable edition | | DeepSeek Harness | Portable edition | | Hermes Agent | Portable edition | See the [local guide](docs/local/usage.md) for each host's entry point and [editions](docs/local/editions.md) for the differences. Source lives in [`local/`](local/). Local runs the built-in workflows today; exporting a platform SOP for standalone local execution is planned. | | Platform | Local | | --- | --- | --- | | Best for | Teams sharing chat workspaces, SOPs, approvals and history | One developer inside an IDE or CLI | | Needs | Docker + Python 3 | Node.js 20+, Python 3.8+ and a coding assistant | | Workflows | Chat with Main Bot + custom SOPs on a visual canvas | Built-in Classic / Portable workflows | | Evidence | Shared run details, approvals and metrics in the web workspace | Artifacts under `artifacts/{task_slug}/` + optional local dashboard | ## FAQ **Do I need an API key to try it?** No. The demo SOP uses only a script and a human gate. Chat and agent steps need a key for the executor you pick. Model usage is not included; you bring your own credentials. **Do I need GitHub?** No. Chat, documents and new projects run in the task workspace. Connect GitHub when you want to change an existing repository or open PRs. **Should I use chat or an SOP?** Use chat to explore and iterate; Main Bot can still open a PR. Once you find a way of working you want every requirement to follow, with fixed reviewers, tests and sign-off, put it in an SOP. Main Bot can start, pause and take over SOP runs, so the two paths work together. **How is this different from Dify, n8n or Flowise?** Those are general-purpose AI and automation workflow builders. LoopForge is built for **software delivery with coding agents**: implementer and reviewer roles, Docker sandboxes with real repositories, GitHub delivery, human acceptance gates and run evidence. **How is this different from using Claude Code, Codex, CodeBuddy or another coding CLI directly?** LoopForge doesn't replace them; it orchestrates them. Each agent step and each chat turn runs one of those CLIs. LoopForge adds what surrounds it: who does what, in which sandbox, in which order, with which checks, and who signs off. **Is it safe to expose on the internet?** New installations listen on all interfaces and target a trusted team. Read the [account and access model](docs/deployment.md#accounts) and set up HTTPS before opening it up. Report vulnerabilities privately via the [security policy](SECURITY.md). ## Documentation | I want to… | Start here | | --- | --- | | Deploy, manage accounts, connect execution machines | [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) | | Understand chat workspaces, scheduled AI tasks and token pricing | [Conversation workspaces](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) · [AI scheduled tasks](docs/ai-scheduled-task-capabilities.md) · [Token pricing](docs/token-pricing.md) | | Install local workflows or choose an edition | [LoopForge Local](docs/local/usage.md) · [Editions](docs/local/editions.md) | | Extend the platform or use the HTTP / MCP API | [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) · [API reference](docs/api/README.md) · [Shared schedules API](docs/api/shared-schedules.md) | | Contribute to the UI | [Frontend design conventions](design.md) (Chinese) | | Check functional coverage and release readiness | [Validation record](docs/validation.md) · [Acceptance matrix](docs/testing/acceptance-matrix.md) · [Release review](docs/release-readiness.md) | | Understand source provenance and maintenance | [Public scope](docs/open-source-scope.md) · [Upstream synchronization](docs/upstream-sync.md) | ## Community Scan the QR code to join the LoopForge community group. ## Contributing Issues and PRs are welcome: share a use case, report a bug, or improve workflows, integrations and the platform experience. Start with the [contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md). Security issues go through the [security policy](SECURITY.md). If LoopForge is useful to you, a star helps others find it. ## License [MIT](LICENSE). Third-party components keep their own licenses and notices; see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

repositories.name: open-code-review
repositories.description: Secure, fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.
repositories.readme:
OpenCodeReview

English | 简体中文 | 日本語 | 한국어 | Русский

--- ## What is Open Code Review? Open Code Review is an AI-powered code review CLI tool. It originated as Alibaba Group's internal official AI code review assistant — over the past two years, it has served tens of thousands of developers and identified millions of code defects. After thorough validation at massive scale, we incubated it into an open source project for the community. Simply configure a model endpoint to get started. It reads Git diffs, sends changed files to a configurable LLM via an agent with tool-use capabilities, and generates structured review comments with line-level precision. The agent can read full file contents, search the codebase, inspect other changed files for context, and produce deep reviews — not just surface-level diff feedback. Beyond diff review, `ocr scan` reviews entire files for auditing unfamiliar codebases or directories that have no meaningful diff. Visit the [official website](https://open-codereview.ai) for more details. ![Highlights](imgs/highlights-en.png) ## Benchmark > Compared to general-purpose agents (Claude Code), Open Code Review achieves significantly higher **Precision** and **F1** with the same underlying model, while consuming only **~1/9 of the tokens** and completing reviews faster. Note that its Recall is lower than general-purpose agents — a deliberate trade-off favoring precision over noise. A real-world code review benchmark built from **50** popular open-source repositories, **200** real Pull Requests, and **10** programming languages — cross-validated by 80+ senior engineers (**1,505** annotated ground-truth issues). Explore the AACR-Bench dataset on Hugging Face. | Metric | What it measures | Why it matters | |--------|-----------------|----------------| | **F1** | Harmonic mean of precision and recall | Best single number for overall review quality | | **Precision** | Proportion of reported issues that are real defects | Higher = fewer false alarms to triage | | **Recall** | Proportion of real defects that are found | Higher = fewer issues slip through review | | **Avg Time** | Wall-clock time per review | Matters for CI pipeline latency | | **Avg Token** | Total tokens consumed per review | Directly impacts API cost | ![Benchmark](imgs/benchmark-en.png) ## Why Open Code Review? ### The Problem with General-Purpose Agents If you've used general-purpose agents like Claude Code with Skills for code review, you've likely encountered these pain points: - **Incomplete coverage** — On larger changesets, agents tend to "cut corners," selectively reviewing only some files and missing others. - **Position drift** — Reported issues frequently don't match the actual code location, with line numbers or file references drifting off target. - **Unstable quality** — Natural-language-driven Skills are hard to debug, and review quality fluctuates significantly with minor prompt variations. The root cause: a purely language-driven architecture lacks hard constraints on the review process. ### Core Design: Deterministic Engineering × Agent Hybrid Open Code Review's core philosophy is to combine deterministic engineering with an agent, each handling what it does best. **Deterministic Engineering — Hard Constraints** For review steps that *must not go wrong*, engineering logic — not the language model — guarantees correctness: - **Precise file selection** — Determines exactly which files need review and which should be filtered, ensuring no important change is missed. - **Smart file bundling** — Groups related files into a single review unit (e.g., `message_en.properties` and `message_zh.properties` are bundled together). Each bundle runs as a sub-agent with isolated context — a divide-and-conquer strategy that stays stable on very large changesets and naturally supports concurrent review. - **Fine-grained rule matching** — Matches review rules to each file's characteristics, keeping the model's attention sharply focused and eliminating information noise at the source. Compared to purely language-driven rule guidance, template-engine-based rule matching is more stable and predictable. - **External positioning and reflection modules** — Independent comment-positioning and comment-reflection modules systematically improve both the location accuracy and content accuracy of AI feedback. **Agent — Dynamic Decision-Making** The agent's strengths are concentrated where they matter most — dynamic decisions and dynamic context retrieval: - **Scenario-tuned prompts** — Prompt templates deeply optimized for code review, improving effectiveness while reducing token consumption. - **Scenario-tuned toolset** — Distilled from deep analysis of tool-call traces in large-scale production data — including call frequency distributions, per-tool repetition rates, and the impact of new tools on the overall call chain — resulting in a purpose-built toolset that is more stable and predictable for code review than a generic agent toolkit. ## How to Use ### Prerequisites - **Git >= 2.41** — Open Code Review relies on Git for diff generation, code search, and repository operations. ### Agent Skills Use the skills in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Kimi Code, or another agent that supports Agent Skills and can run local commands. Both modes require **Git >= 2.41** and the **`ocr` CLI**; only native mode requires an OCR model provider. #### 1. Install the Skills Run in the project you want to review, then select the skills you need and your agent in the installer: ```bash npx skills add alibaba/open-code-review ``` The skills guide your agent to install `ocr` if it is missing, subject to your environment's permissions. You can also install it ahead of time with `npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review`. Prefer a plugin or manual installation? See the [agent-specific setup guide](plugins/open-code-review/README.md), or copy the desired folders from [`skills/`](skills/) into your agent's skill directory. #### 2. Choose a Review Mode | | Native mode | Delegation mode | |---|---|---| | Skill | [`open-code-review`](skills/open-code-review/SKILL.md) | [`open-code-review-delegate`](skills/open-code-review-delegate/SKILL.md) | | Who reviews? | OCR's specialized review agent and pipeline | Your current coding agent, following OCR's review pipeline and guardrails | | Model and authentication | OCR's own provider configuration | Your host agent's existing model and authentication | | Choose it when | You have a model endpoint for OCR and want its full review pipeline | You have no separate API key, or want to use your existing agent subscription/setup | **No separate key? Start with delegation mode.** It skips OCR provider setup, not the host agent's own authentication, usage limits, or costs. A host-agent subscription is not automatically an API credential for native mode. In delegation mode, OCR's CLI and skill together provide the review pipeline and guardrails: file selection, rule resolution, coverage requirements, and structured reporting. The host agent performs analysis, positioning, and reporting within that workflow; it does not run OCR's full native pipeline. For native mode, configure a provider once with `ocr config provider` and `ocr config model`. Authentication depends on the provider; see [Configuration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration). ### CLI #### Install ```bash npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review ``` After installation, the `ocr` command is available globally. For other installation methods (install script, GitHub Release binary, from source), see [Installation](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/installation). #### Quick Start **1. Configure LLM** You must configure an LLM before reviewing code, unless you use [Delegation Mode](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/delegate). - **OCR calls the model:** `ocr review`, the `/open-code-review:review` command, and the `open-code-review` skill use OCR's own provider configuration, not your Claude Code Team/Pro subscription login. Authentication requirements depend on the provider; see [Configuration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration). - **The host agent calls the model:** the `/open-code-review:delegate-review` command and the `open-code-review-delegate` skill use the host agent's configured model and authentication. No separate LLM configuration or credentials are needed in OCR. See the [Claude Code install steps](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#claude-code). ```bash ocr config provider # Select a built-in provider or add a custom one ocr config model # Pick a model for the active provider ``` ![Model providers](imgs/providers.jpg) The interactive UI guides you through provider selection, API key entry, and model configuration, then automatically tests connectivity. For CLI setup, environment variables, custom providers, and other advanced configuration, see [Configuration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration). **2. Review** ```bash cd your-project # Workspace mode — review all staged, unstaged, and untracked changes ocr review # Branch range — reviews feature-branch's changes since it diverged from main (merge-base mode) ocr review --from main --to feature-branch # Single commit ocr review --commit abc123 # Resume an interrupted range or commit review ocr session list ocr review --from main --to feature-branch --resume # Full-file scan — review whole files instead of a diff (no git history needed) ocr scan # scan the entire repository ocr scan --path internal/agent # scan a directory or specific files ocr scan --resume # resume an interrupted full-file scan # Save results to a file (recommended for AI host agents) ocr review --format json --output result.json # Delegation mode — let your AI coding agent perform the review itself # OCR handles file selection and rule resolution; no LLM configuration needed ocr delegate preview ocr delegate rule src/main.go src/handler.go ``` ## Documentation Full documentation lives at **[open-codereview.ai/docs](https://open-codereview.ai/docs)**: - [Quickstart](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/quickstart) — install and run your first review - [Installation](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/installation) — all platforms and package managers - [CLI Reference](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/cli-reference) — every command and flag - [Review Rules](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/review-rules) — customize review rules with path filtering and targeting - [Configuration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration) — config keys and environment variables - [MCP Server](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/mcp) — extend the review agent with external tools - Coding Agent Integrations — choose the platform you use - [Claude Code](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#claude-code) — install a plugin with review slash commands - [Codex](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#codex) — install a plugin with callable review skills - [Cursor](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#cursor) — install a plugin with portable review skills - [Kimi Code](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#kimi-code) — install a plugin with review slash commands and skills - [OpenCode](plugins/open-code-review/opencode/README.md) — install native review tools and slash commands - [QCA Forward](plugins/open-code-review/qca/README.md) — run delegation mode with the QCA host model and a ready-to-publish template - [Skill-compatible agents](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/agent-skill) — install the portable agent skill - Review Execution Modes — after integration, choose which LLM performs the review - [Default (OCR-managed)](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration) — OCR runs the review using its configured LLM - [Delegation Mode](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/delegate) — your coding agent runs the review using its own LLM; no OCR API key required - [CI/CD Integration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/cicd) — GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, GitFlic CI, and Gerrit integration - [Session Viewer](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/viewer) — browse and replay review sessions in browser, mark comments as fixed or ignored and hide them while you work through the findings - [Telemetry](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/telemetry) — OpenTelemetry integration for observability - [FAQ](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/faq) — common questions and troubleshooting ## Contributing This project exists thanks to all the people who contribute. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup, coding guidelines, and how to submit pull requests. ## License [Apache-2.0](LICENSE) — Copyright 2026 Alibaba

# Chrome DevTools for agents

[![npm chrome-devtools-mcp package](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/chrome-devtools-mcp.svg)](https://npmjs.org/package/chrome-devtools-mcp)

Chrome DevTools for agents (`chrome-devtools-mcp`) lets your coding agent (such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor or Copilot)
control and inspect a live Chrome browser. It is available as a
Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server and as a [CLI][cli]. Both give your AI
coding assistant access to the full power of Chrome DevTools for reliable
automation, in-depth debugging, and performance analysis.

[Tool reference][tool-reference] | [CLI][cli] | [Skills][skills] | [Changelog][changelog] | [Contributing][contributing] | [Troubleshooting][troubleshooting] | [Design Principles][design-principles]

## Key features

- **Get performance insights**: Uses [Chrome
  DevTools](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/devtools-frontend) to record
  traces and extract actionable performance insights.
- **Advanced browser debugging**: Analyze network requests, take screenshots and
  check browser console messages (with source-mapped stack traces).
- **Reliable automation**. Uses
  [puppeteer](https://github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer) to automate actions in
  Chrome and automatically wait for action results.

## Disclaimers

`chrome-devtools-mcp` exposes content of the browser instance to the MCP clients
allowing them to inspect, debug, and modify any data in the browser or DevTools.
Avoid sharing sensitive or personal information that you don't want to share with
MCP clients.

`chrome-devtools-mcp` officially supports Google Chrome and [Chrome for Testing](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-for-testing/) only.
Other Chromium-based browsers may work, but this is not guaranteed, and you may encounter unexpected behavior. Use at your own discretion.
We are committed to providing fixes and support for the latest version of [Extended Stable Chrome](https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule).

Performance tools may send trace URLs to the Google CrUX API to fetch real-user
experience data. This helps provide a holistic performance picture by
presenting field data alongside lab data. This data is collected by the [Chrome
User Experience Report (CrUX)](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux). To disable
this, run with the `--no-performance-crux` flag.

## **Usage statistics**

Google collects usage statistics (such as tool invocation success rates, latency, and environment information) to improve the reliability and performance of Chrome DevTools MCP.

Data collection is **enabled by default**. You can opt-out by passing the `--no-usage-statistics` flag when starting the server:

```json
"args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest", "--no-usage-statistics"]
```

Google handles this data in accordance with the [Google Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy).

Google's collection of usage statistics for Chrome DevTools MCP is independent from the Chrome browser's usage statistics. Opting out of Chrome metrics does not automatically opt you out of this tool, and vice-versa.

Collection is disabled if `CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_USAGE_STATISTICS` or `CI` env variables are set.

## Update checks

By default, the server periodically checks the npm registry for updates and logs a notification when a newer version is available.
You can disable these update checks by setting the `CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_UPDATE_CHECKS` environment variable.

## Requirements

- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) [LTS](https://github.com/nodejs/Release#release-schedule) version.
- [Chrome](https://www.google.com/chrome/) current stable version or newer.
- [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/)

## Getting started

Add the following config to your MCP client:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> Using `chrome-devtools-mcp@latest` ensures that your MCP client will always use the latest version of the Chrome DevTools MCP server.

### MCP Client configuration

For setup instructions specific to your editor or agent (e.g. Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code), please see our [Client Configurations Guide][client-configurations-guide].

### Your first prompt

Enter the following prompt in your MCP Client to check if everything is working:

```
Check the performance of https://developers.chrome.com
```

Your MCP client should open the browser and record a performance trace.

> [!NOTE]
> The MCP server will start the browser automatically once the MCP client uses a tool that requires a running browser instance. Connecting to the Chrome DevTools MCP server on its own will not automatically start the browser.

## CLI

The package also includes the `chrome-devtools` CLI. Use it to control the browser from your terminal without MCP:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
chrome-devtools navigate_page 1 --url "https://developers.chrome.com"
chrome-devtools take_screenshot 1 --filePath screenshot.png
chrome-devtools stop
```

See the [CLI guide][cli] for all commands and options.

## Skills

The package includes [skills](./skills) that teach your agent how to use Chrome DevTools:

| Skill                                                     | Use it to                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| [`chrome-devtools`](./skills/chrome-devtools)             | Debug and automate pages with the MCP tools.    |
| [`chrome-devtools-cli`](./skills/chrome-devtools-cli)     | Run the CLI and write shell scripts with it.    |
| [`a11y-debugging`](./skills/a11y-debugging)               | Audit and fix accessibility issues.             |
| [`cookie-debugging`](./skills/cookie-debugging)           | Debug cookies, sessions, and authentication.    |
| [`debug-optimize-lcp`](./skills/debug-optimize-lcp)       | Debug and improve Largest Contentful Paint.     |
| [`memory-leak-debugging`](./skills/memory-leak-debugging) | Find and fix memory leaks.                      |
| [`troubleshooting`](./skills/troubleshooting)             | Fix connection problems between MCP and Chrome. |

### Install skills as a plugin

A plugin installs the MCP server and all skills, including the CLI skill:

- **Claude Code:** Run `/plugin marketplace add ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`, then `/plugin install chrome-devtools-mcp@chrome-devtools-plugins`.
- **Copilot / VS Code:** Run **Chat: Install Plugin From Source** and enter `ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`.
- **Gemini CLI:** Run `gemini extensions install --auto-update https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`.

See the [Client Configurations Guide][client-configurations-guide] for more information.

### Install skills manually

If your agent does not support plugins, copy the skill folders into the skills directory of your agent. The npm package contains the skills:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
# Example for Claude Code. Use the skills directory of your agent.
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The `chrome-devtools-cli` skill requires the CLI. Install the package globally before you use the skill.

### Keep skills up to date

Skills describe the tools of a specific version. Update the skills each time you update the MCP server or the CLI. Outdated skills can tell your agent to use tools or parameters that changed.

- **Plugins:** Use the update command of the plugin manager of your agent. The Gemini CLI command above enables automatic updates with `--auto-update`.
- **Manual installs:** Update the package, then copy the skill folders again:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/
```

## Tools

If you run into any issues, checkout our [troubleshooting guide][troubleshooting].
See the full [Tool Reference][tool-reference] for a complete list of all supported MCP capabilities.

## Configuration

Find the complete list of server parameters (e.g., `--headless`, `--isolated`, `--slim`) and how to configure WebSocket connections in the [Configuration Guide][configuration-guide].

For basic browser tasks only, the `--slim` flag exposes a reduced set of tools. See the [Slim tool reference][slim-tool-reference].

## Advanced Usage

For advanced features such as handling concurrent sessions, persistent user data directories, using a custom or non-standard browser path (`--executablePath`), connecting to a running Chrome instance instead of starting a new one, or debugging on Android, see our [Advanced Usage Guide][advanced-usage-guide].

## Integrating as a browser subagent

If you are developing agentic tooling and want to provide an integrated browser subagent as part of your product, we recommend building on top of Chrome DevTools for agents.

For a reference implementation, see the [Gemini CLI browser agent documentation](https://geminicli.com/docs/core/subagents/#browser-agent).
